data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: What’s the deal with 800V? Why the EV tech that only matters some of the time should not be at the top of your shopping list
data.description:
Read a press kit for many new electric cars revealed recently and you could find a reference to 800 volts in it somewhere.

BMW’s new iX3 (pictured above). The Mercedes-Benz CLA. Porsche’s soon-to-arrive Cayenne Electric. Various cars from Zeekr, XPeng, Lotus and more.

Of course, the Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron GT and various Kias and Hyundais have been using 800V architectures for years.

But recently the default is very much turning to the higher voltage.

Eight hundred volts is presented as a leap forward, and in one sense it is.

But it’s also arguably a tad over-hyped, at least for the vast majority of the time for most EV owners.

What 800V really means

An EV battery is a stack of individual cells wired together.

Each cell typically puts out somewhere around 3.6 volts for NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) batteries, or around 3.2V for LFP (lithium ferrous phosphate) batteries.

Wire them in series and the voltages add up; wire them in parallel and the capacity adds up.

They’ll still have the same amount of energy, but how they absorb and disperse it can be different.

Arrange them one way and you get a pack of around 400V, which is what most EVs have utilised until recently.

Arrange them another way and you can step the voltage up to 800 or more.

Even then, the voltage an EV puts out varies depending on how much charge is in the battery.

And the voltage is rarely 800V.

The Porsche Taycan is the car that started it all, yet even though it’s badged as an 800-volt system the original cars had a nominal voltage of 613V for the smaller battery and 723V for the larger battery.

And for that larger battery the voltage can swing from about 610 volts when flat to about 835 volts when full.

Voltage rises as state of charge rises, which is how the car monitors how much charge is left.

So an 800V system is not so much a hard and fast measurement, in the same way the 12V batteries used in all cars rarely put out 12 volts; they usually hover around  12.6 volts and get pushed to 14V or higher when the car is running.

When you see claims of how fast a car can charge it will often be relying on a high voltage – in the case of the upcoming Porsche Cayenne that’s 850V – and a lot of current (the amps required to get the power up).

Voltage ain’t power, but it helps achieve it

Anyone who remembers their high school physics will know that electrical power equals voltage multiplied by amps.

Ultimately, it’s the power that determines how fast the car will charge – but a higher voltage makes it easier to produce more power.

If you want to push 350kW into a battery at 400V, you need 875 amps. That’s a lot.

Push the same 350kW at 800V and you need less than 440 amps.

Compare that with the 10A maximum that a home powerpoint can put out and you can see we’re talking about big hits of electricity.

And those amps – the current – is the problem.

Current generates heat, and heat is the enemy of everything in the charging chain: including the cables and various connectors.

That’s why high-power charging cables can be liquid-cooled and very thick (and, therefore, heavy).

Double the current and you quadruple the resistive losses. Halve it and those losses drop off a cliff.

So doubling the voltage lets you move a lot more energy through the same hardware.

The main benefit with 800V is DC fast charging

An 800V architecture is almost entirely about public DC fast charging.

It affects almost nothing else with your ownership experience.

Charging at home on AC is identical no matter what the voltage of the battery pack.

Your home powerpoint – or EV charger – puts out about 230V, which is a whole heap less than what the battery is rated at.

It also goes through the car’s onboard charger to convert it from AC electricity coming out of the wall to DC electricity to be stored in the battery pack.

That onboard charger is typically 7kW, 11kW or 22kW, regardless of pack voltage.

An 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 and a 400V Tesla Model Y plugged into the same wallbox overnight will do exactly the same thing at exactly the same rate.

For anyone charging predominantly at home – which is most EV owners, most of the time – 800V is a number on a brochure.

However, there are some secondary benefits.

Lower current means thinner cables and less copper inside the car, which saves a few kilograms and some cost.

For Porsche, the lower weight is important.

It’s a company that has built its reputation on performance, so every little bit counts.

Higher voltages also mean slightly lower losses under sustained high load.

That’s one reason electricity is transported at extremely high voltages (sometimes 500,000V) over big distances.

For Porsche and others chasing big performance, the higher voltage can help with repeatable track performance rather than just charging.

Really, though, the headline is faster charging.

Are there downsides to an 800V electrical system?

Higher voltage is harder and more expensive to engineer.

Every high-voltage component – inverters, DC-DC converters, compressors, contactors, insulation, connectors – has to be rated for the extra stress.

Silicon carbide semiconductors rated to 1200V are one solution, but they cost more than those used in a 400V EV.

Higher voltages also mean greater insulation to ensure safety.

And the big one: if the charger you’re using is limited to 400V then there’s zero benefit.

In some instances there could be negatives.

Roll up to the latest 300kW Tesla Supercharger, for example, and the limiting factor could be the current (amp) limit on the car.

The Hyundai Ioniq 5/6/9 are a good example.

Their DC charging typically tops out at about 320kW, which is 400A of current.

The cabling in the car, therefore, is limited to 400A, which at 400V is 160kW.

Similarly, the Porsche Macan is rated at up to 270kW of fast charging, but only on 800V. At 400V it’s limited to 135kW, again due to those current limits.

So even though the cars are capable of higher-powered charging, it relies on the 800V system to achieve that.

Can an 800V EV use a 400V charger?

All EVs can use all fast chargers, no matter what the voltage of the charger or what voltage the car is rated at.

That’s thanks to some simple but clever designs that allow the electrons to sort themselves out and everything to work as intended.

But there are different ways of achieving it.

The simplest way – and the way used by the Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron and latest Mercedes-Benz CLA – is to use a DC-to-DC booster.

It steps the voltage up so that the battery sees 800V.

With its latest Macan, Porsche did without the need for that booster, instead essentially splitting the battery into two 400V banks and charging them concurrently when it sees a 400V load.

Hyundai and Kia used something quite clever, employing the motor as an inverter.

The rear inverter is reconfigured to act as a boost converter and the rear motor’s windings do the job of the inductor.

So there’s no additional hardware, no extra weight, although presumably there’s some tricky software to ensure it all works the way it should.

800V charging is limited, for now

Here’s where the enthusiasm needs tempering.

Australia’s ultra-rapid network – the 350kW and 450kW units from the likes of Evie, Chargefox, NRMA, Ampol and BP – will generally deliver above 800V and let an 800V EV maximise its charging speed.

But the far bigger slice of Australia’s public charging infrastructure is 400V, often limited to 50kW and 75kW hardware.

That includes the vast Tesla Supercharger network, much of it now open to all EVs.

That’s because all Teslas sold in Australia run a 400V system (the Cybertruck is the brand’s first 800V EV).

Tesla’s reasoning is that bigger, higher-draw vehicles benefit, smaller EVs with smaller batteries less so.

The other half of the answer is that Tesla built its way around the problem. Rather than raising voltage, it went hard on current: Model 3 and Model Y peak at 250kW on a 400V system.

Tesla owns its charging network, so it had the advantage of being able to optimise both ends of the equation.

Is it inevitable Tesla changes? Probably, but it’ll likely happen when a new platform demands it.

Why not go to 1000V or 2000V?

Higher voltage is generally better, right?

In many instances, yes, but it also creates challenges.

BYD’s Super e-Platform is a full 1000V architecture, paired with a battery capable of charging at up to 1000A, for a peak of 1000kW.

That’s the tech behind the “flash charging” sites Denza has committed to installing at Australian dealerships.

So, if 800 is better than 400, why isn’t everyone at 1500V or higher?

Essentially it comes down to safety.

We’ve all seen lightning, which is a high voltage burst of electricity travelling through thin air.

Air is an insulator, but only up to a point.

Push enough voltage across a gap and the air itself ionises and becomes conductive – you get an arc.

The higher the voltage, the wider the gap it can jump.

No amount of clever software gets around it.

Engineers solve the issue by providing more clearance – distance – between high voltage components where you don’t want a spark.

Go higher in voltage and components have to physically move further apart, in a car where nobody has spare room.

There’s also the issue of the plug.

The CCS2 Combo plug fitted to every EV now sold in Australia – including Teslas – tops out at 1000V.

Anything beyond means a new connector standard, which the EV world (rightly) is not in a rush to adopt.

Components dealing with higher voltages can also get expensive.

Besides, with circa-300km charging now down to 10 minutes or less – and BYD/Denza’s flash charging to halve that – it’s getting to the point where the gains are minimal.

Will all brands end up on 800V?

More and more cars are embracing 800V electrical systems, but not because 800V is magic.

It’ll happen because new platforms get designed once and live for a decade, because silicon carbide is getting cheaper every year, and because no car maker wants to be the one whose spec sheet says 400 when the rival’s says 800.

With bigger and more luxurious EVs it’s a no-brainer to head to 800V.

But we’d still expect cheaper city-focussed cars to stay 400V for a while yet, because an LFP hatchback with a 50kWh battery charging at 80kW has nothing to gain.

One point worth making is :don’t go buying an EV based on the voltage.

Buy it because of how it suits your needs and if the charging achieves what you need it to in terms of time taken.

A car that hits 350kW for 90 seconds and then falls off a cliff is not as good as one that sits at 180kW from 10 to 70 per cent.

The post What’s the deal with 800V? Why the EV tech that only matters some of the time should not be at the top of your shopping list appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Lepas L4 makes Australian debut as new Chery brand’s ambitious five-model rollout takes shape
data.description:
Chery’s newest Australian brand Lepas has publicly shown its second model, the L4 electric SUV, as it prepares to unleash an unusually rapid rollout of EVs and plug-in hybrids stretching into 2028.

The compact L4 made its Australian public debut alongside the larger L6 at Everything Electric Sydney last weekend, ahead of an expected local launch in December 2026.

But the L4 is only one part of a much broader expansion plan for Lepas, which intends to establish a five-model family in Australia comprising a small hatchback and small, medium, large and extra-large SUVs.

The assault starts with the L6 EV in October, followed only two months later by the L4 EV.

Plug-in hybrid versions will quickly follow, with the L6 PHEV scheduled for March 2027 and L4 PHEV for June.

The larger L8 PHEV is due in September 2027, while the flagship L9 PHEV is scheduled for the second half of 2027. Battery-electric L8 and L9 variants are planned for 2028, when the smaller L2 hatchback is also expected with battery-electric and hybrid powertrains.

Lepas Australia chief operating officer Lucas Harris said at a media preview ahead of Everything Electric that the brand intended to have almost its entire initial range here by the end of 2027.

“We will have five cars initially. A small hatchback, and then a small, medium, large and extra-large SUV. Every one of them battery electric or plug-in hybrid,” Harris said.

“The first car will arrive in the fourth quarter … and then by the end of 2027, we’ll have the full range just about here, maybe the last one early 2028.”

The L4 is particularly significant because it will give Lepas an entrant in one of the most hotly contested parts of the Australian EV market.

It has also now appeared in the federal government’s ROVER vehicle homologation database, adding new Australian-specification details to those announced by Lepas.

The Road Vehicle Descriptor identifies the vehicle by its internal T371 model code and its Lepas 4/L4 marketing designation. At this stage only a front-wheel drive battery-electric variant is listed.

The five-seat SUV measures 4420mm long, 1817mm wide and 1629mm high, with a relatively lengthy 2700mm wheelbase and 171mm of ground clearance.

The Australian homologation filing also reveals a 1750kg tare weight and 2256kg gross vehicle mass, along with a 1250kg braked towing capacity and 750kg unbraked limit.

The Australian L4 is listed with 18-inch wheels and 215/55 R18 tyres.

Its single front-mounted electric motor produces 160kW, a figure confirmed both by Lepas Australia and the ROVER documentation.

Harris said the L4 would use the same 65kWh lithium iron phosphate battery and 160kW motor as the larger L6, but stretch its claimed WLTP range to 450km.

“450 kilometres of range, same battery, same power, a little bit shorter overall, but the same wheelbase,” Harris said.

“So you’ll get the space and [an] easier car to park in it. It goes a little further than the L6, but nothing has been taken out of it.”

The L6 is claimed to travel 440km from the same 65kWh battery and develops 275Nm from its 160kW motor.

Underpinning the range is Lepas’s LEX architecture, which the company says was designed from the outset for electrified vehicles rather than being adapted from a combustion-engine platform.

Battery-electric models are being positioned as the priority, with plug-in hybrid alternatives planned across most of the range.

Lepas is one part of a rapid expansion of the wider Chery group in Australia. Chery and Jaecoo are already established here, while iCaur and the Chery-JLR Freelander brand are also headed to Australia. Jetour is another Chery-owned brand bound for Australia, although it will be managed separately.

Pricing for the L4 and L6 has yet to be announced.

The post Lepas L4 makes Australian debut as new Chery brand’s ambitious five-model rollout takes shape appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Chinese premium brand Avatr confirms first Aussie model: 07L electric SUV deliveries will start in 2027
data.description:
Chinese luxury brand Avatr has confirmed the 07L electric SUV will lead its Australian launch, with pre-orders due to open before the end of 2026 and first customer deliveries targeted for the first half of 2027.

The right-hand-drive five-seater will be revealed in Australian specification ahead of pre-orders. The parent Changan Group is handling the local introduction, but pricing, the number of variants and the sales and service arrangements have not been announced.

The 07L is a larger model than the Avatr 07 SUV previously identified as a potential Australian candidate after a right-hand-drive example was photographed testing in Melbourne. Avatr lists the 07L at 4910mm long and 1980mm wide, with a 2990mm wheelbase. The earlier 07 measures 4825mm long with a 2940mm wheelbase.

READ MORE: Another Chinese auto giant is coming to Australia: Changan and luxury Avatr prepare EV and PHEV assault
READ MORE: Yep, yet another Chinese brand is coming to Australia: Luxury Avatr confirmed with its line-up of SUV and saloon EVs and range extenders.
READ MORE: 2026 Beijing Auto Show Greatest Hits: All the PHEVs, EVs, supercars and mega SUVs that will change the automotive game this year

While Avatr has not confirmed which versions Australia will receive, its global specification sheet lists three all-electric 07L variants. All use an 89.33kWh CATL lithium iron phosphate battery and an 800-volt electrical architecture.

Two rear-wheel-drive versions produce 305kW and 435Nm, accelerate from 0–100km/h in a claimed 5.9 seconds and have a quoted 725km driving range under China’s CLTC test cycle.

The three-motor all-wheel-drive flagship produces a combined 712kW and 996Nm, reaches 100km/h in a claimed 3.7 seconds and has a quoted 650km CLTC range.

Avatr claims a zero-to-80 per cent DC charging time of 20 minutes and a 30-to-80 per cent time of less than 10 minutes for the global variants. It also claims a 10-minute charge can add 375km of CLTC range. Australian charging specifications and a locally applicable driving-range figure have yet to be published.

The global equipment list includes a wide digital display environment, Meridian audio and available electronic exterior mirrors.

Avatr says its operating system has been localised for Australia, but final equipment and driver-assistance functions will depend on local specification and approval.

Avatr also sells petrol-powered range-extender vehicles overseas. Its Australian announcement commits to the battery-electric 07L; it does not confirm other models or powertrains for this market.

The brand is backed by Changan, with battery maker CATL among its major investors and Huawei a technology partner.

Its Australian debut will add another Chinese contender to a premium EV market that already includes Zeekr and BYD’s Denza brand.

Changan is already connected to the Australian market through Deepal, which is distributed locally by Inchcape.

Changan says it will lead Avatr’s launch, with further details on the 07L’s Australian specifications, pricing and ownership arrangements expected ahead of orders opening later this year.

The post Chinese premium brand Avatr confirms first Aussie model: 07L electric SUV deliveries will start in 2027 appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: What is going on with BYD? Shark 6 under scrutiny as recall and hacking headlines collide with booming sales
data.description:
BYD Australia has vowed to investigate allegations its popular Shark 6 plug-in hybrid ute can be hacked, as it responds to the latest in a series of high-profile issues to hit the fast-growing Chinese brand.

The cybersecurity concerns follow a major safety recall affecting 32,009 Shark 6s and come only months after BYD admitted more than 1200 Australian customers had been sold vehicles built in a different year to that stated on their contracts.

The latest issue emerged from an ABC Four Corners investigation in which cybersecurity researcher Dan Hreszczuk gained access to systems in a Shark 6 and demonstrated he could remotely operate several vehicle functions.

READ MORE: 2026 BYD Seal 6 Touring Brief Drive: Ferociously good value with city-friendly space
READ MORE: BYD M9 lands from $61,990: Forget other Chinese people-movers, the M9 is aimed straight at the top-selling Kia Carnival
READ MORE: History made! $19,990 BYD Atto 1 becomes Australia’s cheapest new car as EV price war hits new low

“We take the allegations very seriously as vehicle security and safety of our customers and all road users is paramount. We are conducting our own investigations,” BYD Australia told EV Central.

“It appears the vulnerability does not exist without first gaining unrestricted access to the vehicle. This will form part of the investigation.”

Hreszczuk was given access to the Shark 6 for two weeks and discovered a digital access point he said was not protected by a password.

He subsequently demonstrated access to functions including the lights, wipers, infotainment system and speakers while the vehicle was being driven.

The investigation also reported access to the vehicle’s location and microphone.

However, Hreszczuk was unable to access more safety-critical systems including the brakes and cameras, which he described as well protected.

That distinction is important because BYD is not disputing that access to vehicle functions was demonstrated. Instead, its response raises questions over whether the vulnerability could be exploited without an attacker first gaining unrestricted access to the vehicle.

The investigation comes amid growing scrutiny of the amount of data collected by increasingly connected new vehicles and how securely that information is stored and transmitted.

The issue is not confined to BYD or Chinese manufacturers, with cameras, microphones, smartphone apps, mobile data connections and over-the-air software increasingly commonplace across the global new-car industry.

BYD says Australian customer data is stored in Australia and has previously said it has not and would not hand Australian customer data to Chinese authorities.

The cybersecurity allegations have emerged at an awkward time for the Shark 6, which is also subject to a federal safety recall covering 32,009 vehicles built from 2024 to 2026.

The Department of Infrastructure says a manufacturing defect may have resulted in the spare-wheel tray or lifter being incorrectly positioned, potentially causing its support cable to wear and fracture.

If the cable fails, the spare wheel could detach from the vehicle while driving, increasing the risk of an accident causing injury or death.

BYD will rectify affected vehicles free of charge through its dealer network.

The size of the recall is significant given about 30,000 Shark 6s have been reported sold in Australia since the PHEV ute launched here.

Both issues follow a separate controversy in July when BYD admitted 1265 Australian customers had been sold 2025-built vehicles despite contracts and other documentation identifying them as 2026 builds.

The affected vehicles included the Shark 6, Atto 3 electric SUV and Sealion 8 plug-in hybrid SUV.

BYD blamed an administrative error in which the date vehicles left the factory was used instead of their actual manufacturing date.

The company said there was no difference in specification, safety, warranty or performance, but acknowledged the build-year discrepancy could affect resale values.

After initially offering affected owners $1100 compensation, BYD subsequently offered remedies including a full refund or the opportunity to purchase a replacement 2026-built vehicle.

The cybersecurity investigation, recall and build-year error are separate issues and there is no evidence they share a common cause.

They have nevertheless emerged as BYD becomes an increasingly significant player in the Australian new-car market.

BYD sold 8231 vehicles in August and 68,423 in the first eight months of 2026, while simultaneously applying significant downward pressure to EV and PHEV pricing.

Its latest move has been to push the Atto 1 electric hatch below $20,000 drive-away, while the new Atto 2 DM-i has reset the entry point for plug-in hybrid vehicles.

The Shark 6 has played a major role in that expansion. It effectively established the mainstream PHEV ute market in Australia and remains a strong seller, recording 1385 deliveries in August and 12,094 for the year to date.

But competition is intensifying, with the Ford Ranger PHEV, JAC Hunter PHEV and GWM plug-in hybrid utes now providing alternatives in a segment the Shark 6 initially had largely to itself.

The post What is going on with BYD? Shark 6 under scrutiny as recall and hacking headlines collide with booming sales appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: BYD has done it again! Atto 2 DM-i becomes Australia’s cheapest PHEV at $24,990
data.description:
BYD has cut the entry price for a new plug-in hybrid in Australia to $24,990 before on-road costs with the launch of the Atto 2 DM-i small SUV.

The front-wheel-drive Atto 2 DM-i comes in Essential and Premium grades, priced at $24,990 and $29,990 respectively. The Essential is $9000 less than BYD’s Sealion 5, which previously held the cheapest-PHEV title at $33,990 before on-road costs.

The plug-in hybrid is also cheaper than the electric Atto 2. The DM-i Essential costs $7000 less than the $31,990 Atto 2 Dynamic EV, while the DM-i Premium undercuts the $35,990 Atto 2 Premium EV by $6000.

READ MORE: BYD M9 lands from $61,990: Forget other Chinese people-movers, the M9 is aimed straight at the top-selling Kia Carnival
READ MORE: History made! $19,990 BYD Atto 1 becomes Australia’s cheapest new car as EV price war hits new low
READ MORE: 2026 BYD Atto 2 Dynamic Review: Cheap and surprisingly cheerful compact electric SUV makes ICE rivals redundant

The pricing follows BYD’s recent move to offer the electric Atto 1 for less than $20,000 drive-away. At $24,990 before on-road costs, the new PHEV sits among Australia’s cheapest new cars regardless of powertrain.

It matches the list price of a manual Suzuki Swift Hybrid, although an exact position in the overall price rankings is difficult to state when some rivals publish drive-away prices and others quote prices before on-road costs.

Both DM-i versions combine a 1.5-litre petrol engine with a 145kW front electric motor. BYD lists combined system outputs of 122kW for the Essential and 156kW for the Premium, with 300Nm for both.

Those system figures are lower than the motor’s quoted peak output because their respective peaks are not necessarily available at the same time.

The Essential has a 7.85kWh battery and a claimed 39km of electric driving under WLTP testing. The Premium’s larger 18.03kWh battery increases that figure to 90km.

BYD quotes combined petrol and electric ranges of 845km and 895km respectively, and 0–100km/h times of 9.1 and 7.5 seconds.

Charging is limited to 3.3kW AC in both grades. BYD says charging from 15 to 100 per cent takes 2.7 hours for the Essential and 6.1 hours for the Premium. Only the Premium has vehicle-to-load capability, with up to 3kW available to run external devices.

The official combined fuel consumption claims are 1.8L/100km for the Essential and 0.7L/100km for the Premium when the batteries have sufficient charge. As with other PHEVs, fuel use will depend heavily on how often owners plug them in.

At 4330mm long, the five-seat Atto 2 DM-i has a claimed 425-litre boot, expanding to 1335 litres with the rear seats folded. Both versions are rated to tow 750kg with a braked trailer and have a listed 490kg payload.

Standard equipment includes a 360-degree camera, adaptive cruise control, autonomous emergency braking, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and an 8.8-inch driver display. The Essential has a 10.1-inch central touchscreen and fabric seats.

The Premium adds a 12.8-inch screen, synthetic leather upholstery, heated front seats, a panoramic sunroof and a 50W wireless phone charger.

The Atto 2 DM-i’s closest price rival is another BYD. The Sealion 5 starts at $33,990 before on-road costs, followed by the Seal 6 sedan at $34,990 and Geely Starray EM-i at $37,490. The Leapmotor B10 Hybrid EV starts at $37,888.

Prices for several other affordable PHEVs are published on a drive-away basis, so direct dollar comparisons require care.

data.title: Saudi Arabia’s first car brand reveals crazy 1111hp EVs … and then confirms it won’t stay EV-only
data.description:
Saudi Arabia’s first home-grown car brand has revealed its first production models, and it certainly hasn’t taken a conservative approach.

The new Ceer Exobot has been unveiled as both a large electric sedan and SUV, with flagship versions developing as much as 1111hp – about 828kW – and 1500Nm from a tri-motor all-wheel drive system.

Ceer claims the most powerful Exobot sedan can accelerate from 0-100km/h in just 2.1 seconds and reach 250km/h, while the SUV requires 2.4 seconds and tops out at 210km/h.

READ MORE: Eight new EV brands you’ve never heard of – and they don’t come from China

But the initial Exobot First Edition models are slightly less extreme, producing 850hp (about 625kW) and 1000Nm. They still dispatch 0-100km/h in a claimed 2.6 seconds in sedan form and 2.9 seconds as an SUV.

Both use a 112kWh NCM battery and 800-volt electrical architecture, with Ceer claiming a maximum 670km NEDC range for the sedan and 560km for the SUV. A 10-80 per cent DC recharge is claimed to take less than 30 minutes.

There is also a significant change of strategy accompanying Ceer’s first production reveal. Although the company was established in 2022 as Saudi Arabia’s first electric vehicle brand, CEO Jim DeLuca has confirmed its future line-up will extend beyond battery-electric vehicles to include plug-in hybrids and combustion-engined models.

Ceer plans seven models over the next five years, starting with the Exobot sedan and SUV before expanding into smaller and more affordable vehicles. The move reflects a broader shift among global car-makers towards more flexible powertrain strategies as EV demand develops at different rates around the world.

Ceer was established as a joint venture between Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF), and Taiwanese electronics manufacturing giant Foxconn.

Ceer is a central part of Saudi Arabia’s push to establish its own automotive manufacturing industry as the oil-rich kingdom attempts to diversify its economy.

The Exobot certainly looks designed to attract attention. Both versions feature a dramatic wedge-shaped profile and enormous upward-opening doors that Ceer calls Shahin Wings, inspired by the flight of the Shahin falcon.

The doors are almost three metres long and open through a claimed 60cm arc. There is also no conventional B-pillar separating the front and rear passenger compartments.

Another standout feature is a huge 2.4-metre windscreen mounted at a 15-degree angle, while the lighting incorporates 32 individual bars referencing 1932, the year Saudi Arabia was unified as a kingdom.

They’re big cars too. The sedan measures 5260mm long, 2100mm wide and 1430mm high, while the SUV stretches 5020mm long, is also 2100mm wide and stands 1690mm tall.

Foxconn has been involved with the electrical architecture, while Ceer has a technology licensing agreement with BMW. Other suppliers reportedly include Croatian EV specialist Rimac Technology for the rear electric drive unit and Hyundai Transys for the front motors.

Ceer nevertheless says the Exobot has been designed and engineered in Saudi Arabia specifically for the region’s demanding conditions.

That includes what it calls Halo Cooling, which is claimed to reduce cabin temperature from 65 degrees Celsius to 32 degrees within 10 minutes. Special glass coatings and dual front and rear air-conditioning systems are also intended to cope with extreme heat.

Chassis technology includes steer-by-wire, rear-wheel steering, active chassis systems and continuous torque vectoring. The steer-by-wire system reduces steering movement from a conventional 400 degrees to just 160 degrees.

Inside, there’s a 48-inch curved 8K display stretching across the dashboard, supplemented by a 10.4-inch central control screen and an 8.0-inch rear passenger display.

An AI-based voice assistant operates in Arabic and English, while the vehicles also offer over-the-air software updates, digital-key functionality, remote parking and a range of driver assistance systems.

Production will take place at Ceer’s new manufacturing complex at King Abdullah Economic City in Saudi Arabia, which the company describes as the largest automotive production facility in the Middle East.

Sales of the Exobot are expected to begin in Saudi Arabia in early 2027, initially with the limited First Edition before the more configurable Exobot Plus follows.

The company is expected to expand into neighbouring markets from 2028 before progressively broadening its reach through the Middle East and North Africa. However, DeLuca says Ceer’s coming mainstream models are being engineered to meet global regulatory requirements, potentially opening the door to wider exports later. There is no indication Australia is currently part of Ceer’s plans.

Ceer’s arrival has been some time coming. When EV Central first reported on the company in 2023, it was targeting its first production vehicles for 2025.

The post Saudi Arabia’s first car brand reveals crazy 1111hp EVs … and then confirms it won’t stay EV-only appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: EV owners back road-user tax: But AEVA also says petrol and diesel vehicles should pay it too
data.description:
Australia’s leading electric vehicle consumer advocacy group has backed the introduction of road-user charging, but says EV drivers should not be singled out and every vehicle on Australian roads should ultimately pay.

The Australian Electric Vehicle Association (AEVA) is calling for a nationally consistent road-user charge overseen federally, with the amount motorists pay determined by both the distance they travel and the weight of their vehicle.

Under the proposal, petrol, diesel, hybrid and electric vehicles would face the same basic charging system, while fuel excise would remain in place for petrol and diesel vehicles as an additional charge reflecting their emissions.

READ MORE: https://evcentral.com.au/unplugged-ev-buying-incentives-to-be-reduced-as-sales-spiral-not-everyone-is-happy/
READ MORE: Why the FBT exemption for EVs isn’t under threat … yet. And why there’s every chance you’ll be paying a road user charge soon
READ MORE: Don’t do it Jim! Stupid road user charge will be a disaster for the EV market in Australia | Opinion

AEVA says more than 85 per cent of its members support its proposed model.

The proposal comes as Australian governments grapple with how to replace revenue expected to decline as motorists progressively move away from petrol and diesel vehicles.

Federal, state and territory treasurers agreed in September 2025 to progress work on road-user charging, saying reforms should provide fair and sustainable funding for roads without deterring EV uptake. However, the Commonwealth has not settled the design or timing of a national scheme.

AEVA argues that if two vehicles of the same weight travel the same distance, they should incur the same road-user charge regardless of whether they are powered by petrol, diesel or electricity.

“If two vehicles weigh the same, and are driven the same distance each year, it’s only fair that they pay the same road user charge,” AEVA policy convenor Dr Chris Jones said.

“But if one of those vehicles burns petrol or diesel, they should pay for the cost of that pollution too.”

AEVA’s policy favours a mass-multiplied distance charge, so a heavier vehicle would pay more per kilometre than a lighter one. The association argues this better reflects road wear and would also encourage buyers towards lighter, more efficient vehicles.

The proposal is particularly relevant in NSW, where legislation provides for an EV road-user charge to begin on July 1, 2027, or earlier if battery-electric vehicles reach 30 per cent of new light-vehicle sales.

For 2026-27, the legislated NSW rates are 3.095 cents per kilometre for battery-electric and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles and 2.476 cents per kilometre for plug-in hybrids.

But whether that scheme can proceed in its existing form remains unresolved. The NSW Government says it is still assessing the implications of the 2023 High Court decision that struck down Victoria’s EV road-user charge after finding the state levy amounted to an excise.

AEVA argues the NSW approach would create anomalies because it considers distance and powertrain but not vehicle weight.

“The NSW model means an EV would pay more per kilometre than a conventional petrol hybrid,” Jones said.

“It also means an electric motorcycle would pay the same rate as a 3-tonne electric SUV, despite having a negligible impact on infrastructure.”

The more contentious element of AEVA’s proposal is its treatment of fuel excise.

Rather than simply replacing fuel excise with a road-user charge, AEVA wants excise retained for combustion-engine vehicles, describing it as effectively a pollution tax on petrol and diesel consumption.

Fuel excise has been particularly politically sensitive in 2026. The Federal Government more than halved excise for three months to June 30 as part of temporary fuel-price relief, then reduced it by 16 cents per litre until August 2 before rates returned to their pre-relief settings.

AEVA says the objective is not to give EV drivers a free ride, but to ensure the eventual road-funding system does not specifically penalise electric vehicles.

“We knew this was coming, so we’ve spent the last decade both leading the debate and advocating for a fair implementation,” Jones said.

“We’re not after a free ride, but we are asking for policy which encourages EV adoption and motivates better vehicle choices.”

The post EV owners back road-user tax: But AEVA also says petrol and diesel vehicles should pay it too appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Volvo splits its future in two as EV and PHEV model blitz responds to a divided world. But what happens in Australia?
data.description:
Volvo is radically reshaping its future EV and plug-in hybrid line-up, splitting development between Western markets and China as tariffs, technology restrictions and diverging customer tastes bring the era of the global car under increasing pressure.

The Swedish brand has announced its biggest-ever product offensive, with 13 all-new electrified models due by the end of 2030 – seven developed for Western markets and six specifically for China.

But where Australia fits into that increasingly divided Volvo world remains unclear.

READ MORE: Volvo EX60 Australian pricing and line-up confirmed: All-new, high-tech electric SUV undercuts BMW iX3
READ MORE: Price slash! Volvo takes the axe to EX30 and EX40 pricing. Up to $11,300 off!
READ MORE: Volvo EX30 Cross Country hits Australia: Do we need an EV soft-roader that’s faster than a Porsche 911 GT3?

Volvo Car Australia told EV Central it could not discuss that level of detail at this stage when asked whether Australia would be classified as a Western market or potentially have access to China-developed models.

The distinction matters because the two groups of vehicles will increasingly have different technical foundations.

Western-market models will use Volvo’s SPA2 and newer SPA3 architectures and its HuginCore technology stack. The China-specific models will make much greater use of parent company Geely, including shared platforms and components and a dedicated Eastern technology stack.

Volvo says deglobalisation – driven by trade tariffs, technology restrictions and increasingly different customer preferences – is behind the strategy.

The company hasn’t revealed the identity of its 13 new cars, but has provided some important clues.

Europe is heading towards a full battery-electric line-up by 2030, although Volvo will supplement its EVs with what it calls third-generation hybrids to cater for markets and customers transitioning more slowly away from combustion power.

The next all-new European Volvo is due in 2027, while the future range is also expected to expand beyond Volvo’s current SUV-heavy line-up with lower-riding models, potentially including new sedans and/or wagons.

The US strategy includes a new D-segment electric SUV and larger vehicles, while China will get a combination of new EVs and PHEVs.

China is particularly interesting from an Australian perspective. Volvo already builds cars there and Australia increasingly sources vehicles from China, but Volvo’s six new Chinese models are being designed specifically around the requirements of that market.

Right-hand-drive production could therefore determine whether Australia can access them.

If the China-specific cars remain left-hand drive, Australia would be reliant on the Western portfolio, which will need to cater for other RHD markets including the UK.

Volvo did not specifically address Australia during its three-hour global strategy presentation.

The company’s increasingly important PHEV strategy is already becoming apparent. Last week Volvo revealed substantially upgraded versions of the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrid SUVs, with claimed WLTP electric ranges stretching to 200km for the XC60 and 160km for the XC90.

Both long-range PHEVs are scheduled to reach Australia in the second quarter of 2027.

Updated versions of the ageing XC40 mild-hybrid and EX40 electric SUV are also coming here during 2027, while the much more important all-new EX60 electric SUV is joining the Australian range.

Volvo sees these new-generation long-range PHEVs as a bridge for customers who are not yet prepared to switch completely to battery power, while continuing to argue that pure-electric vehicles represent its long-term direction.

The new product strategy also comes with a changing of the guard.

Current Skoda boss Klaus Zellmer has been appointed Volvo president and CEO and will take over no later than October 1, 2027, replacing Håkan Samuelsson.

Samuelsson previously led Volvo from 2012 to 2022 before returning in April 2025 following the departure of Jim Rowan to develop the strategy Zellmer will now inherit.

Volvo’s next generation will also introduce a new design direction. Returning design chief Thomas Ingenlath has confirmed a concept will be revealed during Volvo’s centenary year in 2027 to preview the look of future models.

The upheaval comes at an important time for Volvo in Australia. Local sales have fallen from a record 11,128 vehicles in 2023 to 8898 in 2024 and 7239 in 2025, while 4711 had been sold to the end of August 2026.

The post Volvo splits its future in two as EV and PHEV model blitz responds to a divided world. But what happens in Australia? appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Is this Zeekr’s next big thing in Australia? 7GT shooting brake confirmed with up to 670km range and 500kW flagship
data.description:
Zeekr has locked in its sleek 7GT electric shooting brake for Australia, confirming a three-model line-up with up to 670km of WLTP range, ultra-fast charging and a 500kW flagship capable of hitting 100km/h in just 3.1 seconds.

The low-slung five-door made its Australian debut at Everything Electric Sydney last weekend and will launch in the fourth quarter of 2026. The range comprises RWD, Long Range RWD and Performance AWD variants. Orders are due to open later this year ahead of first customer deliveries in the first quarter of 2027.

Pricing is yet to be announced, but media reports indicate each version of the 7GT will be positioned below the equivalent member of the popular Zeekr 7X SUV line-up.

READ MORE: 2026 Zeekr 7GT Review: Sleek sporty wagon set to arrive with sharp pricing to tempt buyers from a Tesla Model 3 or Toyota Camry
READ MORE: Australia’s safest? New BMW iX3 and Zeekr 7GT EVs become first vehicles to earn five stars under toughest-ever NCAP tests
READ MORE: Sleek four-door Zeekr 7GT wagon launches in right-hand drive: Next stop Australia?

The 7X currently starts from $57,900 before on-road costs, meaning the 7GT will emerge as one of Australia’s more attainable premium electric wagons.

The 7GT becomes Zeekr’s fourth Australian model after the X compact SUV, 7X SUV and 009 people-mover. Designed at the brand’s Gothenburg design centre in Sweden, it is built on Zeekr’s 800-volt Sustainable Experience Architecture (SEA), with buyers able to choose between two battery sizes and rear- or all-wheel drive.

The entry-level RWD pairs a 75kWh lithium iron phosphate battery with a rear-mounted electric motor producing 335kW and 520Nm. Zeekr claims 525km of WLTP range, 0-100km/h in 5.2 seconds and a 10-80 per cent DC recharge in as little as 11 minutes.

The Long Range RWD retains the same 335kW and 520Nm output but upgrades to a 100kWh battery, extending claimed WLTP range to 670km while trimming the sprint to 100km/h to 5.0 seconds.

At the top of the range, the dual-motor Performance AWD delivers 500kW and 790Nm, enough for a claimed 3.1-second 0-100km/h time while still offering up to 590km of WLTP range. It also gains active air suspension with continuously controlled damping and exclusive Sport+ drive mode.

The flagship’s combination of 500kW and 3.1-second acceleration places it firmly in premium performance EV territory, lining up against cars such as the Tesla Model 3 Performance while also challenging mainstream electric passenger cars including the BYD Seal, Mazda 6e, Kia EV4, Polestar 2 and IM5.

Inside, the 7GT features a 15.4-inch 2.5K mini-LED touchscreen, 13-inch digital instrument display and a 35.5-inch augmented-reality head-up display. Heated, ventilated and massaging 14-way powered front seats, twin 50W wireless phone chargers, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard across the range.

The shooting brake body provides 456 litres of boot space that expands to 1390 litres with the rear seats folded, plus a hidden under-floor storage compartment and ski hatch.

Zeekr Assisted Drive bundles Level 2 driver assistance technologies including adaptive cruise control, autonomous emergency braking, emergency lane keeping, blind-spot monitoring and automated parking functions.

The 7GT has already secured a five-star Euro NCAP safety rating under the latest, more stringent testing protocols, although an Australian ANCAP rating has not yet been announced.

Ownership will be backed by a five-year, unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty and five years of roadside assistance.

  • Alongside the 7GT announcement, Zeekr has opened its first standalone body repair centre anywhere in the world in Sydney’s Five Dock. The 2500-square-metre facility adds dedicated repair capability, genuine parts and ADAS calibration as the brand expands its Australian network to more than 25 dealerships by the end of 2026.

The post Is this Zeekr’s next big thing in Australia? 7GT shooting brake confirmed with up to 670km range and 500kW flagship appeared first on EV Central.
